title: Current Affairs — How to Prepare
summary: The static layer of current affairs: how CA questions are framed, the award, sports, summit, day and index categories to track every month, and the pairing-based method to revise them — structure that never expires, whatever the news cycle.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Award and who it is for
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "X award is given for..." or "the highest civilian award".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Order of civilian awards: Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri.
Sports: Arjuna Award = players, Dronacharya Award = coaches.

example.q: The Dronacharya Award is given to whom?
example.solution:
The Arjuna Award is for players
The Dronacharya Award is for the people who train them
Those people are coaches
**Coaches**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The X tournament is related to which sport?" or "how often is it held?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Learn the sport for each cup: Thomas and Uber = badminton, Davis = tennis, Ranji = cricket.
Olympics, Asian Games and the FIFA World Cup come every four years.

example.q: The Thomas Cup is related to which sport?
example.solution:
Thomas Cup is for men's teams
The women's version is the Uber Cup
The sport is badminton
**Badminton**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "The headquarters of X is at..." or "India is not a member of..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
SAARC = Kathmandu, ASEAN = Jakarta, UN = New York, Commonwealth = London.
India is in G20, BRICS, SCO and QUAD. India is not in G7 or NATO.

example.q: Where is the SAARC headquarters?
example.solution:
SAARC is a group of South Asian countries
Its secretariat is in a Himalayan capital
That capital is Kathmandu in Nepal
**Kathmandu**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Important days and what they mark
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "X day is observed to remember..." or "birth anniversary of..."
pyqPatterns.approach:
Person days: 12 Jan = Vivekananda, 5 Sep = Radhakrishnan, 14 Nov = Nehru, 22 Dec = Ramanujan.
Other days: 28 Feb = Science Day, 21 Jun = Yoga Day, 5 Jun = Environment Day.

example.q: National Science Day (28 February) marks which discovery?
example.solution:
28 February is National Science Day
It marks a discovery by C.V. Raman in 1928
That discovery is called the Raman effect
**Raman effect**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Index and the body that publishes it
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Which organisation releases the X index?" or "which pair is wrongly matched".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Match each index to its publisher.
HDI = UNDP, Global Hunger Index = Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe, Gender Gap = WEF, Corruption Index = Transparency International.

example.q: Who publishes the Global Hunger Index?
example.solution:
The Hunger Index is not a UN report
It is made by two NGOs
They are Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe
**Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Who has been appointed as...?" or "who appoints the Governor / CJI / CEC?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Note each new person with their post in one line.
The President appoints Governors, the CJI, the CEC and the CAG.

example.q: Who appoints the Governor of a state?
example.solution:
Article 155 covers this
The Governor is named by the head of the Union
That head is the President of India
**The President**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Statement questions: pick the correct ones
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two or three numbered statements are given, with one wrong detail mixed in.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Check the easiest statement first (a year, a publisher, a headquarters).
One clearly wrong statement removes every option that contains it.

example.q: 1. NITI Aayog releases the SDG India Index. 2. The Global Hunger Index is a UNDP product. Which are correct?
example.solution:
Statement 1: the SDG India Index is by NITI Aayog, so it is true
Statement 2: the Hunger Index is by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe, so it is false
Only statement 1 is true, so **Statement 1 only**

pyqPatterns.pattern: News item linked to a lasting fact
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A news item is given, and the question asks the fixed fact behind it (publisher, year, ministry).
pyqPatterns.approach:
Link each news item to its lasting fact.
Award = year started, summit = headquarters, index = publisher, day = person or event.

example.q: A news item reports the latest Human Development Report. Which body publishes the HDI?
example.solution:
The news item is one edition of a yearly report
The lasting fact is who publishes it
The HDI is published by the UNDP
**UNDP**

subtopics.title: How current-affairs questions are framed
subtopics.concept: Current affairs (CA) questions turn one news fact into one of four frames: direct recall, match-the-column, statement-based, or a bridge to static GK. Track ten news buckets every month. For each item, note the pair the exam asks, such as person and post, not the whole story. Study the last 6-12 months from one monthly source and revise it three times.

tricks.title: Pairing drill
tricks.body: Read a news item and write its two halves, such as 'X award, field' or 'Y summit, host'. Exams ask the halves, not the story.

example.q: A new Chief Justice is sworn in. What do you note?
steps: Skip the ceremony details.
Note the pair: the post and the person.
Add the static root: the collegium recommends and the President appoints.
example.answer: The post and the person, plus how the appointment is made.

tricks.title: Three reads of one source
tricks.body: Read the monthly compilation once, revise it after a month, and revise it again in exam week.

example.q: You have five CA sources and little time. What is the better plan?
steps: Pick one monthly compilation.
Plan three rounds: first read, after a month, last week.

mistakes.wrong: Reading five sources once each.
mistakes.right: Revise one monthly source three times.

mistakes.wrong: Studying the news story and ignoring the pairing.
mistakes.right: Note the pair the exam asks: person and post, award and field, day and theme.

mistakes.wrong: Assuming CA never links back to static GK.
mistakes.right: Attach every item to its static root, such as an index to its publisher.

mistakes.wrong: Reading opinion pieces and speculation closely.
mistakes.right: Skip them. Chase firsts, superlatives, anniversaries and India items.

mistakes.wrong: In a statement set, judging the whole set by one familiar fact.
mistakes.right: Test each statement alone. Usually one has a planted wrong year, ministry or city.

subtopics.notes:
### The four question frames
An exam never asks the full news story. It takes one fact and puts it in one of four frames.

| Frame | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Direct recall | One fact, four options. "Who won the Y award?" |
| Match-the-column | Pairs such as award and field, day and theme, summit and host, index and publisher |
| Statement-based | Two or three numbered statements. One carries a wrong detail. |
| CA-to-static bridge | The news opens a door to a permanent fact |

> **Example:** A Nobel announcement is news. The question may ask the Nobel categories. That is the bridge frame.

### How to crack each frame
- **Direct recall:** you need the fact itself. Your notes must hold it as a short pair.
- **Match-the-column:** check each pair on its own. One wrong letter kills the whole option.
- **Statement-based:** hunt for the one planted error. It is usually a wrong year, a wrong ministry or a wrong city.
- **Bridge:** a summit leads to the group's members and HQ. A new scheme leads to its ministry.

> **Tip:** In a statement set, test every statement against its static root. The root never changes.

### The ten buckets to track every month
Sort every news item into one of ten buckets.

1. **Appointments and offices:** President, Governors, CJI, service chiefs, regulators, heads of world bodies.
2. **Awards and honours:** Bharat Ratna, Padma, gallantry; Nobel, Magsaysay, Booker.
3. **Sports:** winners, hosts, tournaments, records.
4. **Summits and conferences:** host country, theme, outcomes.
5. **Schemes and launches:** new schemes, portals, missions, extensions.
6. **Defence:** exercise names with the partner country, missiles, new inductions.
7. **Space:** ISRO launches, landings, satellites.
8. **Indexes and reports:** India's rank and the publisher.
9. **Important days:** especially UN days and their yearly themes.
10. **Economy:** RBI policy reviews, budgets, GST Council decisions, big reports.

### The working method
The **window** is the time span an exam draws from. Most exams use the last 6-12 months before the exam date.

- Pick **one** monthly compilation. It covers the window month by month.
- Read it once. Revise it after a month. Revise it again in the last week.
- One source revised three times beats five sources read once.

> **Rule:** Note the pairing, not the story. Person and post. Award and field. Event and host. Day and theme. Index and publisher.

### Attach news to its static root
Every news item has a permanent part. Learn that part once and it serves every future year.

| News type | Static root to learn |
|---|---|
| Award | Its structure and the year it began |
| Summit | The group's members, founding year and HQ |
| Scheme | Its ministry and launch year |
| Important day | The person or event it remembers |
| Index | Its publisher |

Often the static root **is** the answer, even when the question names a recent event.

### What to skip and what to chase
Some news is almost never asked. Skip opinion pieces, ongoing court arguments and speculation.

Other news is asked all the time. Chase **firsts, superlatives** (largest, first, fastest), **anniversaries** and India-specific items.

> **Watch:** Exams ask settled facts. An editorial view can never be a correct option.

patterns.name: The ten tracking buckets
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following is NOT usually asked from current affairs', or which kinds of news to track every month.
steps: Recall the ten buckets: appointments, awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence, space, indexes, days, economy.
Mark opinion, speculation, ongoing court arguments and gossip as rarely asked.
Inside a bucket, prefer firsts, superlatives, anniversaries and India items.
Pick the option that is not a settled fact.
patterns.why: Exams ask settled facts, so anything that is only a view drops out.

example.q: Which type of news is least likely to appear as an exam question?
steps: Appointments, award winners and index ranks are settled facts.
An editorial view is not a fact.
Speculation can turn out false.

patterns.name: Identify the question frame
patterns.howToSpot: The question describes how a news item was asked, or asks which method suits a frame.
steps: List the four frames: direct recall, match-the-column, statement-based, bridge.
One fact with four options is direct recall.
Numbered statements with one wrong detail is statement-based.
Pairs to be matched is match-the-column; news leading to a permanent fact is the bridge.
patterns.why: Each frame has one clear shape, so the shape names the frame.

example.q: A question gives three numbered statements about a summit and asks which are correct. What is the frame?
steps: The question has numbered statements.
Usually two are true and one has a planted error.
Test each one against its static root.

patterns.name: Window and revision method
patterns.howToSpot: How far back to study, how many revisions to plan, or what a monthly compilation should cover.
steps: The standard window is the last 6-12 months before the exam.
Banking mains may use a longer window.
Use one monthly source, revised three times.
Make every revision a pairing drill.
patterns.why: A fixed window and one source keep the load small enough to revise.

example.q: What is the usual preparation window for current affairs in a typical exam?
steps: Most exams draw from recent months, not years.
Monthly compilations cover the span month by month.
example.answer: About the last 6-12 months before the exam

patterns.name: CA-to-static bridging
patterns.howToSpot: A news item is shown and the question asks the permanent fact it connects to.
steps: Name the news type: award, summit, scheme, day or index.
Recall its static root: structure, members and HQ, ministry, person remembered, or publisher.
Answer with the static root, not the event detail.
patterns.why: The static root does not change from year to year, so it is safe to ask.

example.q: A news item says a new Global Innovation Index edition is out. Which permanent fact does it anchor?
steps: It is an index, so the root is the publisher.
The publisher stays the same every edition.
example.answer: The Global Innovation Index is published by WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization).

patterns.name: Pick the exam-worthy detail
patterns.howToSpot: 'While reading this news, which detail should you note', or a news item followed by options of what to remember.
steps: Find the pair inside the news: person and post, award and field, event and host.
Add the static root, such as how the post is filled.
Drop ceremony details, quotes and opinions.
patterns.why: Exams ask the halves of a pair, never the colour of the story.

example.q: A new Chief Justice of India is sworn in. Which detail is most worth noting?
steps: The pair is the post and the person.
The static root is the appointment process.
The venue and guests of the ceremony are not asked.
example.answer: The person and the post, plus the process: collegium recommends, President appoints.

revision: Four frames: direct recall, match-the-column, statement-based, CA-to-static bridge.
Ten buckets: appointments, awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence, space, indexes, days, economy.
Window: the last 6-12 months before the exam.
One monthly compilation, revised three times.
Exams test the pairing: person and post, award and field, day and theme, index and publisher.
Attach every news item to its static root.
Firsts, superlatives and anniversaries score most. Opinion and speculation are rarely asked.

subtopics.title: Award categories to track — structure, not winners
subtopics.concept: Learn the ladders, not the winners. Each group of awards has a fixed order, a starting year and a field. Winners change every year, but the structure stays the same. Once you know the structure, every year's news fits into it.

tricks.title: Ladder memory
tricks.body: Civilian: Ratna, Vibhushan, Bhushan, Shri. Sports: Khel Ratna, Arjuna for players, Dronacharya for coaches.

example.q: What is the fourth-highest civilian honour?
steps: Bharat Ratna is first.
Padma Vibhushan is second, Padma Bhushan third.
The next step down is Padma Shri.

tricks.title: Arjuna plays, Drona teaches
tricks.body: In the Mahabharata, Arjuna was the pupil and Drona the teacher. So Arjuna is for players and Dronacharya for coaches.

example.q: The Dronacharya Award is given to whom?
steps: Drona was a teacher.
In sport, the teacher is the coach.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Param Vir Chakra a civilian award.
mistakes.right: It is the highest wartime gallantry award.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing Dronacharya with Arjuna.
mistakes.right: Dronacharya is for coaches. Arjuna is for players.

mistakes.wrong: Placing Padma Shri above Padma Bhushan.
mistakes.right: Order: Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the wartime and peacetime ladders.
mistakes.right: Wartime: PVC, MVC, Vir. Peacetime: Ashoka, Kirti, Shaurya.

mistakes.wrong: Saying all Nobel Prizes are given in Stockholm.
mistakes.right: The Peace Prize is given in Oslo.

mistakes.wrong: Counting Economics as an original Nobel category.
mistakes.right: It was added in 1969. The first prizes were given in 1901.

subtopics.notes:
### Civilian awards: the ladder
India has four civilian awards, from highest to fourth.

| Rank | Award |
|---|---|
| 1 | Bharat Ratna |
| 2 | Padma Vibhushan |
| 3 | Padma Bhushan |
| 4 | Padma Shri |

All four began in **1954**. The Padma awards are announced on the **eve of Republic Day**.

> **Example:** "The fourth-highest civilian award" is Padma Shri. Count down the ladder.

### Bharat Ratna firsts
The Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian honour. Exams love its "firsts".

| First | Name | Year |
|---|---|---|
| First recipients | C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan, C.V. Raman | 1954 |
| First posthumous | Lal Bahadur Shastri | 1966 |
| First woman | Indira Gandhi | 1971 |
| First sportsperson | Sachin Tendulkar | 2014 |

"Posthumous" means given after the person's death.

### Gallantry awards: two ladders
Gallantry awards honour bravery. There are two separate ladders.

| Level | Wartime | Peacetime |
|---|---|---|
| Highest | Param Vir Chakra | Ashoka Chakra |
| Second | Maha Vir Chakra | Kirti Chakra |
| Third | Vir Chakra | Shaurya Chakra |

The Param Vir Chakra was instituted on **26 January 1950**. Gallantry awards are announced around **Republic Day and Independence Day**.

> **Watch:** "Highest gallantry award" with no qualifier means the Param Vir Chakra.

### Literature, cinema and world prizes
- **Jnanpith Award:** the highest literary honour. First given in **1965** to **G. Sankara Kurup** (Malayalam).
- **Sahitya Akademi Award:** given by the National Akademi of Letters, set up in **1954**.
- **Dadasaheb Phalke Award:** the highest cinema honour. Instituted in **1969**. First winner: **Devika Rani**.
- **Nobel Prizes:** they come from **Alfred Nobel's will (1895)**. First given in **1901**.
- **Ramon Magsaysay Award:** the "Asian Nobel". Instituted in **1957**, presented in **Manila**.
- **Booker Prize:** the leading prize for English fiction. The **International Booker** honours translated works.
- **Oscars (Academy Awards):** given since **1929**.

### The Nobel structure
There are six Nobel categories today.

1. Physics
2. Chemistry
3. Physiology or Medicine
4. Literature
5. Peace
6. Economics, **added in 1969** (the Sveriges Riksbank prize)

The first five are the original prizes. All are given in **Stockholm**, except Peace, which is given in **Oslo**.

> **Tip:** "Which is not an original Nobel category?" The answer is Economics.

### Sports awards: the pyramid
| Award | Given for | Began |
|---|---|---|
| Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna | Highest sporting honour | 1991-92 |
| Arjuna Award | Consistent top performance by players | 1961 |
| Dronacharya Award | **Coaches** | 1985 |
| Major Dhyan Chand Award | Lifetime contribution to sport | 2002 |
| MAKA Trophy | Best **university** | 1956-57 |

The Khel Ratna was earlier the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna. It was **renamed in 2021**.

### How an award question is built
Exams test three layers. All three are permanent.

- **The ladder:** which award is highest.
- **The start:** the year it began, or its first winner.
- **Award and field:** Dronacharya is for coaches, MAKA is for a university.

patterns.name: Civilian awards: ladder and firsts
patterns.howToSpot: 'The highest civilian award', 'the first woman to get Bharat Ratna', ordering the Padma awards, or a first posthumous winner.
steps: Write the ladder: Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri.
Recall the firsts: 1954 trio, Shastri 1966, Indira Gandhi 1971, Tendulkar 2014.
Match the word in the question (woman, posthumous, sportsperson) to its row.
patterns.why: The ladder and four firsts cover almost every civilian-award question.

example.q: The first posthumous Bharat Ratna was given to whom?
steps: Posthumous means after death.
The first such award came in 1966.
It went to the Prime Minister who died at Tashkent.

patterns.name: Sports awards: award and field
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Dronacharya Award is given to', 'the highest sports honour', or 'the MAKA Trophy relates to'.
steps: Khel Ratna is the highest sporting honour.
Arjuna is for players, Dronacharya for coaches.
Dhyan Chand Award is for lifetime contribution. MAKA is for the best university.
Use the start years to cut wrong options: 1961, 1985, 2002.
patterns.why: Each sports award has one field, so a swapped field is easy to spot.

example.q: The Dronacharya Award honours whom?
steps: Drona was a teacher in the Mahabharata.
In sport the teacher is the coach.
Players get the Arjuna Award instead.

patterns.name: Nobel prize structure
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Nobel Peace Prize is given at', 'which category was added in 1969', or 'whose will started the prizes'.
steps: Origin: Alfred Nobel's will of 1895. First prizes: 1901.
Five original categories. Economics was added in 1969.
Venue: Oslo for Peace, Stockholm for the rest.
patterns.why: Two dates and one venue answer most Nobel questions.

example.q: Why is the Nobel Prize in Economics different from the original prizes?
steps: The original prizes came from the 1895 will.
They were first given in 1901.
Economics came later, as the Sveriges Riksbank prize.

patterns.name: Gallantry awards: wartime and peacetime
patterns.howToSpot: 'The highest wartime gallantry award', 'the Ashoka Chakra is given for', or ordering the Chakras.
steps: Wartime: Param Vir, Maha Vir, Vir Chakra.
Peacetime: Ashoka, Kirti, Shaurya Chakra.
Find the word 'wartime' or 'peacetime' in the question.
With no qualifier, 'highest gallantry award' means Param Vir Chakra.
patterns.why: Most wrong options come from the other ladder.

example.q: What is India's highest peacetime gallantry award?
steps: Peacetime points to the second ladder.
Its top step is the Ashoka Chakra.
Kirti and Shaurya Chakra follow it.

patterns.name: Literature, film and world prizes
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Jnanpith Award was first won by', 'the Dadasaheb Phalke Award relates to', or 'the Asian Nobel is'.
steps: Jnanpith is literature: 1965, G. Sankara Kurup.
Dadasaheb Phalke is cinema: 1969, Devika Rani.
Magsaysay is the Asian Nobel: 1957, Manila.
Booker is English fiction. International Booker is translation.
patterns.why: Each prize has one field and one first, so matching settles it.

example.q: The Ramon Magsaysay Award, called the 'Asian Nobel', is presented in which city?
steps: It is an Asian award.
It was instituted in 1957.
It is presented in the Philippines' capital.

patterns.name: Order awards by the year they began
patterns.howToSpot: 'Arrange in chronological order', or 'which award is the oldest' among a list of Indian awards.
steps: Write the year next to each award.
Key years: Bharat Ratna and Padma 1954, Arjuna 1961, Jnanpith 1965, Phalke 1969, Dronacharya 1985.
Sort from earliest to latest.
patterns.why: Start years are fixed facts, so a sorted list gives the answer directly.

example.q: Arrange by year of starting: 1. Jnanpith 2. Bharat Ratna 3. Dronacharya 4. Dadasaheb Phalke
steps: Jnanpith 1965, Bharat Ratna 1954, Dronacharya 1985, Phalke 1969.

revision: Civilian: Bharat Ratna > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri. All from 1954.
Bharat Ratna firsts: 1954 trio; posthumous Shastri 1966; woman Indira Gandhi 1971; sportsperson Tendulkar 2014.
Wartime: Param Vir (1950) > Maha Vir > Vir Chakra. Peacetime: Ashoka > Kirti > Shaurya Chakra.
Jnanpith 1965 (G. Sankara Kurup). Dadasaheb Phalke 1969 (Devika Rani).
Nobel: will 1895, first 1901, Economics 1969, Peace in Oslo.
Magsaysay: 1957, Manila, the 'Asian Nobel'. Booker: English fiction.
Sports: Khel Ratna 1991-92 (renamed 2021), Arjuna 1961, Dronacharya 1985, Dhyan Chand Award 2002, MAKA for universities.

subtopics.title: Sports events and how tournament news is asked
subtopics.concept: Every tournament question uses the same five details: host, motto or theme, mascot, champion, and India's highlight. Note these five for each event in your window. Learn each event's cycle, organiser and first edition once, because they never change.

tricks.title: Cycle split
tricks.body: Every four years: Olympics, Winter Olympics, CWG, Asian Games, FIFA, ODI World Cup. Every two years: T20 World Cup, Thomas and Uber Cups. Every year: IPL, Ranji, Khelo India.

example.q: How often is the T20 World Cup held?
steps: The ODI World Cup is the four-yearly one.
The T20 World Cup is in the two-year group.

tricks.title: First editions in date order
tricks.body: Athens 1896, Chamonix 1924, Hamilton and Uruguay 1930, New Delhi 1951, England 1975.

example.q: Which came first: the first Asian Games or the first Cricket World Cup?
steps: Asian Games: 1951.
Cricket World Cup: 1975.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the two-year T20 World Cup with the four-year ODI World Cup.
mistakes.right: T20 is every two years. ODI is every four years.

mistakes.wrong: Putting the Thomas Cup under football or tennis.
mistakes.right: The Thomas Cup is men's badminton. The Uber Cup is women's badminton.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the first Asian Games in Bangkok.
mistakes.right: The first Asian Games were in New Delhi, 1951.

mistakes.wrong: Calling the Durand Cup a hockey or cricket event.
mistakes.right: It is football, Asia's oldest cup, from 1888.

mistakes.wrong: Saying India's first individual Olympic gold came in hockey.
mistakes.right: Hockey golds are team golds. Abhinav Bindra won the first individual gold in 2008.

subtopics.notes:
### How sports news is asked
Every sports question reuses five details.

1. Host country or city
2. Motto or theme
3. Mascot
4. Champion and runner-up
5. India's performance: medals, records, firsts

Note these five for every event in your window. Learn the **cycle** and **organiser** of each event once.

> **Rule:** The five details change each edition. The cycle, organiser and first edition never change.

### The recurring events and their cycles
A cycle is how often an event is held.

| Event | Cycle | Fixed facts |
|---|---|---|
| Summer Olympics | 4 years | Modern Games from 1896, Athens |
| Winter Olympics | 4 years, offset | First in 1924, Chamonix |
| Paralympics | With the Olympics | For athletes with disabilities |
| Commonwealth Games | 4 years | Began as British Empire Games, 1930, Hamilton |
| Asian Games | 4 years | First in 1951, New Delhi; run by the OCA |
| FIFA World Cup | 4 years | First in 1930, Uruguay |
| Cricket World Cup (ODI) | 4 years | First in 1975, England |
| T20 World Cup | 2 years | India won the first, in 2007 |
| Thomas Cup / Uber Cup | 2 years | Men's / women's badminton team events |
| IPL | Every year | BCCI's T20 league, from 2008 |
| Ranji Trophy | Every year | Indian first-class cricket (1934), named after Ranjitsinhji |
| Khelo India Games | Every year | From 2018; school and university levels |

> **Tip:** Only two items here run every two years: the T20 World Cup and the Thomas and Uber Cups.

### Olympic basics
The modern Olympics began at **Athens in 1896**. **Pierre de Coubertin** revived them.

- The **IOC** (International Olympic Committee) was founded in **1894**. Its HQ is at **Lausanne**.
- The motto is "Citius, Altius, Fortius - Communiter". It means faster, higher, stronger - together.
- "Communiter" (together) was added in **2021**.
- The symbol is **five interlocking rings**.

### India's permanent sports facts
- **1900 Paris:** India's first Olympics. **Norman Pritchard** won two athletics silvers.
- **Hockey:** eight Olympic golds. The run began at **1928 Amsterdam**. The last gold came at **1980 Moscow**.
- **Abhinav Bindra:** first individual Olympic gold, **2008**, 10 m air rifle.
- **Neeraj Chopra:** javelin gold at the Tokyo Games.
- **Cricket World Cup:** first win in **1983** under Kapil Dev at Lord's. Second in **2011** under M.S. Dhoni.
- **T20 World Cup:** India won the first edition, in **2007**.
- **Thomas Cup:** India's first win came in **2022**.

### Oldest and first
Exams like superlatives, which are words like "oldest" or "first".

| Superlative | Answer |
|---|---|
| Asia's oldest football tournament | Durand Cup, 1888 |
| Oldest tennis championship | Wimbledon, 1877 |
| Men's tennis team cup | Davis Cup |

> **Example:** "The Durand Cup is linked to which sport?" Football. It is Asia's oldest football cup.

### How to note a tournament
Write one line per event in your window.

*event, year, host, champion, India's highlight, any record*

A statement question usually swaps **one** item in this line. It is most often a wrong host city or a wrong champion. The other items stay true.

> **Watch:** Check each statement alone. One false detail makes that statement wrong, even if the rest is true.

patterns.name: Tournament to sport or organiser
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Thomas Cup is related to which sport', 'the Ranji Trophy is linked to', or 'which body runs the IPL'.
steps: Recall the cup and sport pairs: Thomas and Uber badminton, Davis tennis, Santosh football, Ranji cricket, Durand football.
Recall organisers: IPL is BCCI; Asian Games is the OCA.
Look for the option with a swapped sport.
patterns.why: The wrong option is usually a real cup placed under the wrong sport.

example.q: The Thomas Cup is associated with which sport?
steps: It is a team event for men.
Its women's version is the Uber Cup.
Both are badminton.

patterns.name: Olympic facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'The modern Olympics began in', 'the IOC HQ is at', 'the Olympic motto is', or questions on rings and founder.
steps: Modern Games: Athens, 1896, revived by Pierre de Coubertin.
IOC: founded 1894, HQ at Lausanne.
Motto: faster, higher, stronger - together. 'Together' added in 2021.
Winter Games: first in 1924 at Chamonix.
patterns.why: A handful of fixed Olympic facts covers most options.

example.q: Where is the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee?
steps: The IOC was founded in 1894.
Its HQ is in Switzerland.

patterns.name: India's permanent sports records
patterns.howToSpot: 'India's first individual Olympic gold', 'how many hockey golds', or 'India first won the Thomas Cup in'.
steps: First Olympics: 1900 Paris, Norman Pritchard.
Hockey: eight golds, 1928 to 1980.
First individual gold: Abhinav Bindra, 2008.
Cricket: 1983 ODI, 2007 T20, 2011 ODI. Thomas Cup: 2022.
patterns.why: These India facts are settled history, so they return every year.

example.q: Who won India's first individual Olympic gold medal?
steps: Hockey golds were team golds.
The first individual gold came in 2008.
It was in 10 m air rifle.

patterns.name: Cycles and first editions
patterns.howToSpot: 'How often is the T20 World Cup held', 'the first Asian Games were held at', or 'the first Cricket World Cup was in'.
steps: Sort the event into four-yearly, two-yearly or yearly.
Recall the first edition: Olympics 1896, Winter 1924, CWG 1930, Asian Games 1951, FIFA 1930, ODI 1975.
Match the year and host to the options.
patterns.why: Cycles and first editions never change, so they are safe to learn once.

example.q: Which city hosted the first Asian Games?
steps: The first Asian Games were in 1951.
They were held on Indian soil.

patterns.name: Champion, host and mascot statements
patterns.howToSpot: Numbered statements that mix one wrong host, champion or sport into true sports facts.
steps: Take each statement alone.
Check the host city and champion first. These are swapped most often.
Then check the sport and the organiser.
Pick the option with only the true statements.
patterns.why: Usually only one detail is planted wrong, so a careful check of each line finds it.

example.q: Consider: 1. The IPL is conducted by the BCCI. 2. The Durand Cup is a hockey tournament. 3. Wimbledon is the oldest tennis championship. Which are correct?
steps: 1 is true: the IPL is BCCI's league.
2 is false: the Durand Cup is football.
3 is true: Wimbledon dates from 1877.

patterns.name: Oldest and first tournaments
patterns.howToSpot: Words like 'oldest', 'first' or 'named after' with a tournament.
steps: Durand Cup: Asia's oldest football cup, 1888.
Wimbledon: oldest tennis championship, 1877.
Ranji Trophy: first-class cricket, named after Ranjitsinhji.
patterns.why: Superlatives are fixed facts and appear often in sports sets.

example.q: Asia's oldest football tournament is which one?
steps: It started in 1888.
It is played in India.

revision: Note five per event: host, motto or theme, mascot, champion, India's highlight.
Olympics 1896 Athens (Coubertin). IOC 1894, Lausanne. Winter Games 1924 Chamonix.
CWG from 1930 Hamilton. Asian Games 1951 New Delhi. FIFA 1930 Uruguay.
ODI World Cup from 1975; India won 1983 and 2011. T20 World Cup every two years; India won 2007.
IPL 2008, Ranji 1934, Khelo India 2018. Thomas and Uber Cups are badminton.
India: first Olympics 1900; eight hockey golds (1928-1980); Bindra 2008; Thomas Cup 2022.
Durand Cup 1888 (football). Wimbledon 1877 (tennis). Davis Cup is men's tennis.

subtopics.title: Summits, groupings and organisations to track
subtopics.concept: For every grouping, learn four things: members, headquarters, founding year and what changed recently. Members and headquarters rarely change, so learn them once. The host city and theme change every summit, so note them in one line each. India is not a member of APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO or OPEC.

tricks.title: HQ trio
tricks.body: SCO sits at Beijing, SAARC at Kathmandu and BIMSTEC at Dhaka. ASEAN at Jakarta is the fourth to learn.

example.q: Where is the BIMSTEC secretariat?
steps: BIMSTEC is the Bay of Bengal group.
SAARC, the other South Asian group, is at Kathmandu.
BIMSTEC is at Dhaka.

tricks.title: Five 'not a member' names
tricks.body: India is outside APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO and OPEC. Any option with one of these is the answer to a 'not a member' question.

example.q: India is not a member of which of these: SCO, BRICS, APEC, BIMSTEC?
steps: SCO, BRICS and BIMSTEC all include India.
APEC is on the 'not a member' list.

mistakes.wrong: Marking India as an APEC member.
mistakes.right: India is not in APEC. It is also outside ASEAN, G7, NATO and OPEC.

mistakes.wrong: Putting SAARC's HQ at Dhaka.
mistakes.right: SAARC is at Kathmandu. Dhaka is the BIMSTEC HQ.

mistakes.wrong: Taking 2008 as the year the G20 was founded.
mistakes.right: The G20 began in 1999 with finance ministers. Leaders' summits began in 2008.

mistakes.wrong: Calling India an ASEAN member.
mistakes.right: India is only a dialogue partner of ASEAN.

mistakes.wrong: Giving UNSC non-permanent members a five-year term.
mistakes.right: Their term is two years. Five is the number of permanent members.

subtopics.notes:
### What a summit question asks
A summit question checks one of four details. They are the host, the members, the headquarters (HQ) and what changed.

Members and HQ stay the same for years. Learn them once. The host city and the theme change with every summit.

> **Example:** "G20, New Delhi, 2023. The African Union joined." One line gives the host, the year and the change.

### The groupings to know
| Grouping | Founded | HQ | Key facts |
|---|---|---|---|
| G20 | 1999 (finance ministers); leaders' summits from 2008 | None; the presidency rotates | 19 countries + European Union; African Union joined 2023 |
| BRICS | Name coined 2001; first summit 2009 | New Development Bank (NDB) at Shanghai | Brazil, Russia, India, China; South Africa 2010; expanded 2024 |
| SCO | 2001, grew out of the Shanghai Five | Beijing (anti-terror unit RATS at Tashkent) | India and Pakistan full members 2017; Belarus 2024 |
| QUAD | 2007, revived 2017 | No HQ | India, USA, Japan, Australia; leaders' meetings since 2021 |
| ASEAN | 1967, Bangkok Declaration | Jakarta | Southeast Asian bloc; India is only a dialogue partner |
| SAARC | 1985, first summit at Dhaka | Kathmandu | 8 South Asian members; SAFTA from 2006 |
| BIMSTEC | 1997 | Dhaka | 7 Bay of Bengal countries |
| Commonwealth | Modern form from the London Declaration, 1949 | London (Marlborough House) | 56 members; the British Sovereign is Head |
| NAM | 1961, Belgrade | No HQ | India is a founding member |

The 2024 BRICS entrants include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE. The seven BIMSTEC members are Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand.

> **Tip:** Three HQs get swapped most: SCO at Beijing, SAARC at Kathmandu, BIMSTEC at Dhaka.

### The United Nations
The UN was founded in **1945** with 51 founding members. It now has **193 members**. Its HQ is in New York. Its main court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), sits at The Hague.

The Security Council (UNSC) has 15 seats:

- **5 permanent** members with a veto: the US, UK, France, Russia and China.
- **10 non-permanent** members, elected for **two-year** terms.

India has been elected a non-permanent member **eight times**. Its latest term was 2021-22. India has long pressed for reform of the Council.

### India in or out
| India is a member | India is not a member |
|---|---|
| UN, G20, BRICS, SCO, QUAD | APEC |
| SAARC, BIMSTEC, Commonwealth, NAM | ASEAN (dialogue partner only) |
| IMF, World Bank, WTO, AIIB, ADB | G7, NATO, OPEC |

India hosts the **International Solar Alliance** with France. Its HQ is at Gurugram. India has at times led the G77, the group of developing countries at the UN.

> **Watch:** APEC is the classic trap. India trades with Pacific countries but is not an APEC member.

### How to note a summit
Write one line per summit: group, host city or country, theme, what changed.

After the host, membership change is the most asked detail. Past examples are the African Union joining the G20, Belarus joining the SCO and the BRICS expansion.

Themes are often slogans. The New Delhi G20 theme was "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam: One Earth, One Family, One Future".

patterns.name: Summit, host and theme
patterns.howToSpot: 'The X summit was hosted by', 'the theme of the summit was', or statements pairing a summit with a city.
steps: Recall your one-line note: group, host, theme, change.
Match the host city first.
If cities are swapped, reject pairs from the wrong region.
For a theme, look for the slogan you noted.
patterns.why: Hosts and themes are the most asked details of any summit.

example.q: The G20 Leaders' Summit hosted by India at New Delhi in 2023 had which theme?
steps: The summit was India's G20 presidency.
Its theme came from an old Sanskrit phrase.
The same summit admitted the African Union.
example.answer: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam: One Earth, One Family, One Future

patterns.name: Grouping, members and headquarters
patterns.howToSpot: 'X is headquartered at', 'how many members does X have', or a match-the-following of groups and cities.
steps: Recall the HQ pins: SCO Beijing, SAARC Kathmandu, BIMSTEC Dhaka, ASEAN Jakarta.
Add NDB Shanghai, Commonwealth London, ISA Gurugram.
Recall counts: SAARC 8, BIMSTEC 7, UN 193, Commonwealth 56.
Cross out any option that swaps two South Asian HQs.
patterns.why: HQs and member counts are fixed, so a short list settles most questions.

example.q: The headquarters of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) is at which city?
steps: The SCO was founded in 2001.
Its secretariat is in China's capital.
Its anti-terror unit, RATS, is at Tashkent, not the HQ.

patterns.name: India's membership: in or out
patterns.howToSpot: 'India is NOT a member of', or statements placing India inside or outside a grouping.
steps: Recall the 'out' list: APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO, OPEC.
Check each option against it.
Remember ASEAN gives India dialogue-partner status only.
patterns.why: The 'out' list has only five names, so it is quicker than the 'in' list.

example.q: India is NOT a member of which of the following? (a) SCO (b) BIMSTEC (c) APEC (d) G20
steps: SCO: India joined in 2017.
BIMSTEC and G20: India is a member.
APEC is on the 'out' list.

patterns.name: Founding years and new members
patterns.howToSpot: 'When did India join the SCO', 'which body joined the G20', or arranging groupings by founding year.
steps: Recall years: UN 1945, NAM 1961, ASEAN 1967, SAARC 1985, BIMSTEC 1997, G20 1999, SCO 2001.
Recall changes: India-Pakistan into SCO 2017, AU into G20 2023, BRICS expansion 2024, Belarus into SCO 2024.
Match the change to the right group before reading other options.
patterns.why: Each change belongs to one group and one year, so pair them as a unit.

example.q: In which year did India and Pakistan become full members of the SCO?
steps: The SCO was founded in 2001.
Both countries were admitted together.
Belarus joined later, in 2024.

patterns.name: UN structure and India at the UN
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many members does the UN have', 'UNSC non-permanent members serve for', or India's UNSC terms.
steps: UN: 1945, 193 members, HQ New York; ICJ at The Hague.
UNSC: 15 seats, 5 permanent with veto plus 10 non-permanent.
Non-permanent terms are two years.
India has been elected eight times; latest term 2021-22.
patterns.why: The UN numbers are fixed and asked again and again.

example.q: Non-permanent members of the UN Security Council are elected for a term of how many years?
steps: The Council has 15 seats.
5 are permanent with a veto.
The other 10 rotate on fixed terms.

patterns.name: Name the grouping from its members
patterns.howToSpot: A list of countries is given and the grouping is asked, e.g. 'India, USA, Japan and Australia form'.
steps: Count the countries in the list.
Four democracies across the Indo-Pacific means QUAD.
Seven Bay of Bengal countries means BIMSTEC.
Eight South Asian countries means SAARC.
patterns.why: Each small grouping has a member list that fits no other group.

example.q: India, the USA, Japan and Australia are the four members of which grouping?
steps: The list has exactly four countries.
It began in 2007 and was revived in 2017.
It has no HQ.

revision: G20: 1999, leaders' summits from 2008, no HQ; African Union joined 2023.
BRICS: first summit 2009; NDB at Shanghai; South Africa 2010; expanded 2024.
SCO: 2001, Beijing; India and Pakistan joined 2017; Belarus 2024.
QUAD: India, USA, Japan, Australia; revived 2017.
ASEAN 1967 Jakarta. SAARC 1985 Kathmandu (8). BIMSTEC 1997 Dhaka (7).
UN 1945, 193 members; UNSC = 5 permanent + 10 non-permanent (two-year terms).
Commonwealth: 56 members, London. NAM: 1961, Belgrade.
India is not in APEC, ASEAN, G7, NATO or OPEC.

subtopics.title: Important days — national and UN framework
subtopics.concept: Each important day marks a person, an event or a global cause. Exams ask what the day marks more often than the date itself. Learn the fixed date and the reason behind it. The yearly theme changes, so note it only for the current year.

tricks.title: Person-day chain
tricks.body: Go by month: 12 Jan Vivekananda, 1 Jul B.C. Roy, 29 Aug Dhyan Chand, 5 Sep Radhakrishnan, 31 Oct Patel, 14 Nov Nehru, 22 Dec Ramanujan.

example.q: National Sports Day honours whom?
steps: National Sports Day is 29 August.
In the chain, 29 August is Dhyan Chand.
The national sports awards are given on this day.

tricks.title: Services by month
tricks.body: Army comes first in the year (15 January), Air Force next (8 October), Navy last (4 December).

example.q: Which service day falls on 4 December?
steps: 4 December is the last of the three dates.
The last one is the Navy.

mistakes.wrong: Treating Constitution Day and Republic Day as the same.
mistakes.right: Constitution Day (26 Nov) marks adoption in 1949. Republic Day (26 Jan) marks it coming into force in 1950.

mistakes.wrong: Linking Teachers' Day to Maulana Azad.
mistakes.right: Teachers' Day (5 Sep) is Radhakrishnan. National Education Day (11 Nov) is Azad.

mistakes.wrong: Putting Air Force Day on 4 December.
mistakes.right: 4 December is Navy Day. Air Force Day is 8 October.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Yoga Day was first observed in 2014.
mistakes.right: The UN declared it in December 2014. It was first observed in 2015.

mistakes.wrong: Learning only the dates.
mistakes.right: Learn who or what each day marks. That is what the question asks.

subtopics.notes:
### Two kinds of day questions
A day question links a date to what it marks. Most national days mark a person's birth or a national event. UN days mark a global cause or a charter.

The date of a day never changes. Its theme changes every year.

> **Example:** 29 August is National Sports Day. It marks the birth of Major Dhyan Chand. The exam asks "whose birth?", not just "which date?".

### Days that honour a person
| Date | Day | Person |
|---|---|---|
| 12 January | National Youth Day | Birth of Swami Vivekananda |
| 1 July | National Doctors' Day | Dr B.C. Roy (birth and death) |
| 29 August | National Sports Day | Major Dhyan Chand |
| 5 September | Teachers' Day | Dr S. Radhakrishnan |
| 31 October | National Unity Day | Birth of Sardar Patel |
| 11 November | National Education Day | Maulana Azad |
| 14 November | Children's Day | Birth of Jawaharlal Nehru |
| 22 December | National Mathematics Day | Srinivasa Ramanujan; since 2012 |
| 25 December | Good Governance Day | Birth of Atal Bihari Vajpayee |

> **Tip:** Read the chain by month: Vivekananda, B.C. Roy, Dhyan Chand, Radhakrishnan, Patel, Nehru, Ramanujan.

### Days that mark an event
| Date | Day | Event |
|---|---|---|
| 28 February | National Science Day | Discovery of the Raman effect (1928) |
| 11 May | National Technology Day | Pokhran tests (11 May 1998) |
| 14 September | Hindi Diwas | Hindi adopted as official language (1949) |
| 26 November | Constitution Day | Constitution adopted (1949); observed since 2015 |

> **Watch:** Constitution Day (26 November) marks adoption in 1949. Republic Day (26 January) marks the Constitution coming into force in 1950.

### The defence trio
- **Army Day, 15 January:** K.M. Cariappa became the first Indian Commander-in-Chief in 1949.
- **Air Force Day, 8 October:** the Indian Air Force was raised in 1932.
- **Navy Day, 4 December:** Operation Trident (1971), the missile attack on Karachi harbour.

The order runs January, October, December.

### UN international days
| Date | Day | Link |
|---|---|---|
| 8 March | International Women's Day | |
| 22 March | World Water Day | |
| 7 April | World Health Day | WHO founded 1948 |
| 22 April | Earth Day | |
| 3 May | World Press Freedom Day | |
| 5 June | World Environment Day | Born of the 1972 Stockholm Conference |
| 21 June | International Day of Yoga | India's proposal |
| 29 July | International Tiger Day | |
| 8 September | International Literacy Day | |
| 2 October | International Day of Non-Violence | Gandhi's birthday |
| 24 October | UN Day | |
| 10 December | Human Rights Day | UDHR adopted 1948 |

Yoga Day is the most asked. The UN declared it in December 2014 on India's proposal. It was first observed in 2015.

### How to study days
1. Learn the **person or event** behind each national day.
2. For UN days, learn the **cause and any Indian link**, such as Yoga Day.
3. Note the **theme** only for days inside your exam window.
4. Anniversaries, like 75 years of the Constitution, fall on these same dates. The fixed date is the anchor.

patterns.name: Day and the person it honours
patterns.howToSpot: 'National Sports Day marks whose birth anniversary', 'Teachers' Day commemorates', or a day-person match.
steps: Identify the day named in the question.
Recall the person from the chain.
Check the date only after you have the person.
Separate Teachers' Day (Radhakrishnan) from Education Day (Azad).
patterns.why: The exam asks the person, not the date alone.

example.q: National Sports Day, observed on 29 August, commemorates the birth anniversary of whom?
steps: 29 August is National Sports Day.
It honours a hockey legend.
The sports awards are given on this day.

patterns.name: Day and the event it marks
patterns.howToSpot: 'National Science Day marks', 'Constitution Day is observed because', or event-days like Pokhran and Trident.
steps: Identify the event-day in the question.
Recall the event and its year: Raman effect 1928, Pokhran 1998, Constitution adopted 1949.
For Constitution Day, remember it has been observed since 2015.
patterns.why: Event-days are asked with the event and often its year.

example.q: National Science Day, observed on 28 February, marks the discovery of what?
steps: 28 February is National Science Day.
It marks C.V. Raman's light-scattering discovery of 1928.
This work later won the Nobel Prize.

patterns.name: UN international days and Indian links
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which day did the UN declare on India's proposal', 'World Environment Day is observed on', or a UN day-date match.
steps: Start with Yoga Day: 21 June, India's proposal, declared 2014, first observed 2015.
Recall the other pins: Environment 5 Jun, Health 7 Apr, Human Rights 10 Dec.
Link each day to its cause: Stockholm 1972, WHO 1948, UDHR 1948.
Treat the yearly theme as a separate, current-year fact.
patterns.why: Yoga Day is the highest-frequency UN day because of its India link.

example.q: The UN declared 21 June as the International Day of Yoga in which year?
steps: India proposed the day.
The UN adopted it in December 2014.
The first Yoga Day was held in 2015.

patterns.name: Defence and service days
patterns.howToSpot: 'Air Force Day is observed on', 'Navy Day commemorates', or the three service days.
steps: Army Day: 15 January (Cariappa, 1949).
Air Force Day: 8 October (raised 1932).
Navy Day: 4 December (Operation Trident, 1971).
Use the order January, October, December.
patterns.why: Only three dates, and the swap between Air Force and Navy is the usual trick.

example.q: Indian Air Force Day is observed on which date?
steps: Army Day is 15 January.
Navy Day is 4 December.
Air Force Day marks the 1932 raising.

patterns.name: Look-alike days
patterns.howToSpot: Two similar days in one question, e.g. 'Constitution Day differs from Republic Day because', or teacher-linked days.
steps: Write the two days side by side.
Recall what each one marks.
Constitution Day: adoption, 1949. Republic Day: in force, 1950.
Teachers' Day: Radhakrishnan. Education Day: Azad.
patterns.why: These pairs share a theme, so only the reason behind each date separates them.

example.q: Constitution Day (26 November) is observed to mark what?
steps: Republic Day (26 January) marks the Constitution coming into force in 1950.
Constitution Day marks the earlier step.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.

patterns.name: Date given, name the day
patterns.howToSpot: Only a date is given: 'Which day is observed on 22 December?' or 'What is celebrated on 11 May?'.
steps: Place the date in the month chain.
Recall the day that sits on it.
Add the person or event to confirm.
patterns.why: Fixed dates make the reverse question as easy as the forward one.

example.q: Which day is observed in India on 22 December?
steps: 22 December is the last person-day before Good Governance Day.
It honours Srinivasa Ramanujan.
It has been observed since 2012.

revision: Youth 12 Jan (Vivekananda), Sports 29 Aug (Dhyan Chand), Teachers 5 Sep (Radhakrishnan).
Unity 31 Oct (Patel), Children 14 Nov (Nehru), Maths 22 Dec (Ramanujan), Good Governance 25 Dec (Vajpayee).
Science 28 Feb (Raman effect), Technology 11 May (Pokhran 1998).
Constitution Day 26 Nov: adopted 1949; observed since 2015.
Army 15 Jan, Air Force 8 Oct, Navy 4 Dec (Operation Trident).
Yoga 21 Jun: India's proposal, UN declared 2014, first observed 2015.
Environment 5 Jun, Health 7 Apr, Non-Violence 2 Oct, UN Day 24 Oct, Human Rights 10 Dec.

subtopics.title: Indexes and reports — index ↔ publisher
subtopics.concept: Index questions mostly ask who publishes an index. Publishers stay the same, while ranks change every edition. Split the publishers into UN bodies, the World Economic Forum, NGOs and Indian bodies. The Global Hunger Index comes from two NGOs, not the UN.

tricks.title: UN or NGO
tricks.body: UN bodies: UNDP (HDI), SDSN (Happiness), WIPO (Innovation), IMF (WEO). NGOs: Concern and Welthungerhilfe (Hunger), IEP (Peace), RSF (Press), Pratham (ASER), TI (Corruption).

example.q: Who publishes the Global Hunger Index?
steps: Hunger sits on the NGO side.
Two NGOs publish it together.
Any UN body in the options is wrong.

tricks.title: WEF trio
tricks.body: Gender Gap, Global Risks, Travel and Tourism: three WEF reports. If an option says WEF for one of these, it is right.

example.q: The Global Gender Gap Report is released by whom?
steps: Gender Gap is one of the WEF trio.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the Global Hunger Index to a UN body.
mistakes.right: Two NGOs publish it: Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the HDI to the World Bank.
mistakes.right: The HDI is UNDP's, inside the Human Development Report.

mistakes.wrong: Quoting last year's rank as current.
mistakes.right: Ranks change every edition. Check the current one; publishers do not change.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing the SDG India Index with the global SDG Index.
mistakes.right: SDG India Index is NITI Aayog. The global one is UN SDSN.

mistakes.wrong: Treating Ease of Doing Business as a live ranking.
mistakes.right: The World Bank stopped it in 2021. B-READY replaced it from 2024.

mistakes.wrong: Reading a higher Corruption Perceptions Index score as more corrupt.
mistakes.right: A higher score means cleaner.

subtopics.notes:
### The publisher is the question
Most index questions ask which body releases which index. India's rank changes with every edition. The publisher does not.

> **Example:** "Global Hunger Index, released by UNDP" is false. Two NGOs publish it.

So learn the publishers first. Note a rank only for the current edition.

### Indexes from UN bodies
| Index | Publisher | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Human Development Index (HDI) | UNDP | Inside the Human Development Report; health, education, income; since 1990 |
| World Happiness Report | UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) | Released in March |
| Global SDG Index | UN SDSN | Tracks the 17 SDGs |
| Global Innovation Index | WIPO, Geneva | Innovation inputs and outputs |
| World Economic Outlook; Global Financial Stability Report | IMF | Flagship reports |
| Human Capital Index | World Bank | Part of the Human Capital Project |

### World Economic Forum reports
The World Economic Forum (WEF) is known for its Davos meeting. It publishes three reports asked in exams:

- Global Gender Gap Report
- Global Risks Report
- Travel and Tourism Development Index

The WEF has paused its Global Competitiveness Report.

### Indexes from NGOs and other bodies
| Index | Publisher |
|---|---|
| Corruption Perceptions Index | Transparency International, Berlin |
| Global Peace Index | Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP), Sydney |
| Global Hunger Index | Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany) |
| World Press Freedom Index | Reporters Without Borders (RSF) |
| Henley Passport Index | Henley and Partners |
| World Competitiveness Index | IMD, Lausanne |
| Environmental Performance Index | Yale and Columbia universities |
| Democracy Index; Global Liveability Index | Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) |

In the Corruption Perceptions Index, a higher score means a cleaner country. The Henley index measures visa-free access. Press Freedom links to World Press Freedom Day on 3 May.

> **Watch:** The Global Hunger Index is the classic trap. Any UN body in the options is wrong.

### India's own indexes
- **NITI Aayog:** SDG India Index, India Innovation Index (with the Institute for Competitiveness), Composite Water Management Index, national Multidimensional Poverty Index.
- **RBI:** Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index) and its Handbook of Statistics.
- **MoSPI:** CPI, IIP and household consumption surveys.
- **Pratham (an NGO):** ASER, the Annual Status of Education Report, on rural schooling.
- **Department of Economic Affairs:** the Economic Survey.

> **Tip:** SDG India Index is NITI Aayog. The global SDG Index is UN SDSN.

### Indexes that ended or changed
The World Bank **discontinued** its Ease of Doing Business ranking in **2021**, after a review of data irregularities. Its successor is **Business Ready (B-READY)**, first released in **2024**.

A question on a retired index usually asks who stopped it and when.

### How to answer
1. Match the publisher first. Wrong options often name the wrong UN body.
2. Sort the body: UN, WEF, NGO or Indian.
3. Check any rank against the current edition only.

patterns.name: Index and its UN publisher
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Human Development Index is released by', 'which body publishes the Global Innovation Index'.
steps: Recall the UN pins: HDI UNDP, Happiness SDSN, Innovation WIPO.
Add WEO IMF and Human Capital World Bank.
Reject options that move an index to another UN body.
Remember the HDI appears inside the Human Development Report.
patterns.why: Wrong options usually swap one UN body for another, so exact pairs matter.

example.q: The Global Innovation Index is released by which organisation?
steps: Innovation is linked to intellectual property.
The UN body for that is WIPO, based in Geneva.
UNDP and the WEF are the usual wrong options.

patterns.name: Index and its non-UN publisher
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Global Hunger Index is released by', 'the Corruption Perceptions Index comes from'.
steps: Recall Hunger: Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe.
Recall Corruption: Transparency International; Peace: IEP; Press: RSF.
Recall Democracy and Liveability: EIU; EPI: Yale and Columbia; Competitiveness: IMD.
If a UN body appears for an NGO index, reject it.
patterns.why: These bodies are not UN agencies, which is exactly what the options test.

example.q: The Global Hunger Index is published by which of the following?
steps: Hunger is an NGO index.
Concern Worldwide is from Ireland.
Welthungerhilfe is from Germany.

patterns.name: Indian indexes and their publishers
patterns.howToSpot: 'The SDG India Index is released by', 'ASER is published by', 'the FI-Index is compiled by'.
steps: NITI Aayog: SDG India, India Innovation, Water Management, national MPI.
RBI: FI-Index. MoSPI: CPI and IIP.
Pratham: ASER. Department of Economic Affairs: Economic Survey.
patterns.why: Indian indexes come from a short list of bodies, each with its own area.

example.q: The SDG India Index is released by which body?
steps: It ranks states and UTs on the 17 SDGs.
The global SDG Index is UN SDSN.
The Indian version comes from the government think tank.

patterns.name: Discontinued and replaced indexes
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Ease of Doing Business index was replaced by', or a statement about a stopped report.
steps: Doing Business: stopped by the World Bank in 2021.
Its successor: Business Ready (B-READY), first released in 2024.
WEF: Global Competitiveness Report paused.
Check who stopped it and when.
patterns.why: Retired indexes test the publisher and the year.

example.q: In which year did the World Bank discontinue its Ease of Doing Business rankings?
steps: A review found data irregularities.
The World Bank stopped the ranking.
B-READY followed from 2024.

patterns.name: World Economic Forum reports
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Global Gender Gap Report is released by', 'Global Risks Report is published by'.
steps: Recall the WEF trio: Gender Gap, Global Risks, Travel and Tourism.
If the index is one of these, choose the WEF.
Do not give Gender Gap to a UN body.
patterns.why: Three reports share one publisher, so one list answers them all.

example.q: The Global Risks Report is published by which organisation?
steps: Global Risks is in the WEF trio.
The other two are Gender Gap and Travel and Tourism.

patterns.name: What an index measures
patterns.howToSpot: 'In the Corruption Perceptions Index, a higher score means', 'the HDI is based on', 'the Henley index ranks'.
steps: HDI: health, education and income.
Corruption Perceptions Index: higher score means cleaner.
Henley Passport Index: visa-free access.
Global SDG Index and SDG India Index: the 17 SDGs.
patterns.why: A few indexes are asked for what they measure, not who publishes them.

example.q: The Human Development Index is built on which three areas?
steps: UNDP publishes the HDI.
It combines a long life, learning and living standard.
Those map to health, education and income.

revision: HDI: UNDP. Happiness and global SDG Index: UN SDSN. Innovation: WIPO.
World Economic Outlook: IMF. Human Capital Index: World Bank.
WEF trio: Gender Gap, Global Risks, Travel and Tourism.
Corruption: Transparency International (Berlin). Peace: IEP. Press Freedom: RSF.
Hunger: Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe (NGOs, not UN).
EPI: Yale + Columbia. Competitiveness: IMD. Democracy, Liveability: EIU.
SDG India and India Innovation Index: NITI Aayog. FI-Index: RBI. ASER: Pratham.
Doing Business ended 2021; B-READY from 2024.

solvedExamples.q:
Match the sports award with its field:
1. Khel Ratna 2. Dronacharya 3. MAKA Trophy
(i) coaches (ii) university (iii) highest sporting honour
solvedExamples.solution: Khel Ratna is the **highest sporting honour** (1991-92, renamed 2021), Dronacharya (1985) goes to **coaches**, and the MAKA Trophy (1956-57) to the best **university**. Work the field column first; the years confirm.

solvedExamples.q: **National Sports Day** is observed on 29 August to mark the birth anniversary of —
solvedExamples.solution: **Major Dhyan Chand**, the hockey wizard — 29 August; the sports awards are conferred the same day. Patel rides 31 October, Nehru 14 November and Vivekananda 12 January.

solvedExamples.q: The **Global Hunger Index** is published by —
solvedExamples.solution: Two NGOs — **Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany)**. Every UN body in the options is the planted trap; the GHI has never been a UN product.

practice.q: A question that gives **two or three numbered statements** and asks which are correct is which frame?
practice.solution: The **statement-based frame** hides one wrong detail (year, ministry, host city) inside mostly true statements — eliminate the planted error and the option set collapses.

practice.q: Pairing **award ↔ field, day ↔ theme, index ↔ publisher** belongs to which frame?
practice.solution: Match-the-column tests **pairs** — the safest method is checking each pair independently; one verified wrong pair eliminates the whole option.

practice.q: In a statement-based CA question, the fastest approach is —
options: Eliminate the option containing a statement with a verified factual error
Read all statements twice, then guess
Choose the option with the most statements
practice.solution: One planted error per set is the norm — a single **verified wrong detail** (wrong year, wrong ministry) knocks out every option containing it.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **standard CA bucket** tracked every month?
practice.solution: Appointments (persons in posts) are one of the **ten fixed buckets** — alongside awards, sports, summits, schemes, defence, space, indexes, days and economy news.

practice.q: Within any news bucket, the items **most frequently asked** are —
practice.solution: Exams love **firsts** (first woman, first Indian), **superlatives** (largest, fastest, highest) and **anniversaries** (X years of an event) — they are precise, checkable and timeless once asked.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Sports winners form a monthly CA bucket.
2. Index ranks and their publishers form a monthly CA bucket.
3. The framing of a pending court case is a common question.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Buckets 1 and 2 are standard. Statement 3 is wrong — **unsettled court arguments and speculation are not asked**; only concluded, factual outcomes appear.

practice.q: The most efficient way to cover a year of current affairs is —
options: One monthly compilation revised multiple times
Reading only the last week's news
practice.solution: **One source, three revisions** (same month, after a month, exam week) — coverage plus retention beats scattered single reads.

practice.q: While noting a **new scheme announcement**, the detail to record for exams is —
practice.solution: Exams ask the **pairing**: which ministry launched it, what it provides, who is eligible. The speech's rhetoric is never the answer.

practice.q: For a **summit** news item, which note is most exam-productive?
options: Host country, theme and membership changes
practice.solution: Summit questions recur on **host, theme, logo, outcomes and new members** — a fixed question shape across years.

practice.q: A news item about a **Nobel Prize** announcement is best revised through —
options: The Nobel prize categories and their structure
practice.solution: The **static root** — six prize categories, Alfred Nobel's will, Peace at Oslo, Economics added in 1969 — serves every year's cycle and often is the tested fact.

practice.q: 'X years of the Constitution' as a news anniversary primarily helps revise —
options: The Constitution's making, parts and Preamble
practice.solution: Anniversaries are bridges to **static topics** — the making of the Constitution, Parts, Schedules and the Preamble — the static layer exams actually test.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about CA preparation:
1. The CA-to-static bridge rewards learning award structures once.
2. Volatile items like a person's current post stay useful only until they change.
3. CA questions never connect to static GK.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — structures endure, offices change. Statement 3 is wrong: the **CA-to-static bridge is one of the four standard frames**.

practice.q: India's **highest civilian award** is —
practice.solution: **Bharat Ratna** (1954) tops the civilian ladder; Param Vir Chakra is a *gallantry* award, not civilian.

practice.q: The **fourth-highest** civilian award of India is —
practice.solution: Order: Bharat Ratna → Padma Vibhushan → Padma Bhushan → **Padma Shri**.

practice.q: The **first woman** to receive the Bharat Ratna was —
practice.solution: **Indira Gandhi (1971)**; Mother Teresa (1980) and Lata Mangeshkar (2001) came later.

practice.q: Padma awards are ordinarily announced on the eve of —
practice.solution: The Padma list is announced on **Republic Day eve** (25 January); gallantry awards also cluster around 26 January and 15 August.

practice.q: The **highest sporting honour** of India is the —
options: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
practice.solution: The **Khel Ratna** (instituted 1991-92, renamed after Major Dhyan Chand in 2021) is the top sports award.

practice.q: The **Dronacharya Award** is given to outstanding —
practice.solution: **Dronacharya (1985) = coaches** — named after the teacher of archery in the Mahabharata; players get the Arjuna Award.

practice.q: The **MAKA Trophy** is awarded to the best —
practice.solution: The **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (MAKA) Trophy** (1956-57) honours the best **university** in sports.

practice.q:
Arrange by instituting year (earliest first):
1. Arjuna Award 2. Dronacharya Award 3. Khel Ratna
practice.solution: Arjuna **1961** → Dronacharya **1985** → Khel Ratna **1991-92** (renamed Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna, 2021).

practice.q: The **Nobel Peace Prize** is awarded in —
practice.solution: Peace is conferred at **Oslo** (by the Norwegian Nobel Committee); all other categories are presented at **Stockholm**.

practice.q: Which Nobel category was **not** part of Alfred Nobel's original will?
practice.solution: Nobel's 1895 will listed five prizes; **Economics** was added in **1969** as the Sveriges Riksbank memorial prize.

practice.q: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in —
practice.solution: Nobel signed his will in **1895**; the first prizes followed in **1901**.

practice.q: India's **highest wartime gallantry award** is the —
practice.solution: **Param Vir Chakra** (instituted 26 January 1950) is the top wartime gallantry medal; Ashoka Chakra heads the peacetime ladder.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **peacetime** gallantry award?
practice.solution: Peacetime ladder: **Ashoka Chakra > Kirti Chakra > Shaurya Chakra**. The MVC and Vir Chakra are wartime medals.

practice.q: The **Jnanpith Award** is associated with —
practice.solution: The **Jnanpith** is India's highest literary honour — first given in **1965** to **G. Sankara Kurup**.

practice.q: The **Dadasaheb Phalke Award**, first given to Devika Rani, honours —
practice.solution: The highest Indian **cinema** honour — instituted **1969**, first recipient **Devika Rani**.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The first Bharat Ratnas were conferred in 1954.
2. The Ramon Magsaysay Award is presented in Manila.
3. The Bharat Ratna can be awarded posthumously.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are correct — the 1954 first batch, the Manila-based Magsaysay (1957), and posthumous conferral (Shastri, 1966) are settled facts.

practice.q: The **Thomas Cup** is associated with —
practice.solution: The **Thomas Cup** is the men's team badminton world championship; women play for the **Uber Cup**.

practice.q: The **Ranji Trophy** is India's premier —
practice.solution: Started **1934** and named after **Ranjitsinhji**, it is the domestic first-class championship; the IPL (2008) is the T20 league.

practice.q: The **Durand Cup**, Asia's oldest football tournament, began in —
practice.solution: The **Durand Cup (1888)** is Asia's oldest football tournament — a favourite superlative question.

practice.q: The **FIFA World Cup** was first held in —
practice.solution: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in **1930**; the tournament runs every four years.

practice.q: The **ICC T20 World Cup** is held —
practice.solution: The T20 World Cup is **biennial**; the ODI World Cup is four-yearly (first 1975).

practice.q: The **Commonwealth Games** began as the British Empire Games in —
practice.solution: First held at **Hamilton, Canada in 1930** as the British Empire Games; four-yearly thereafter.

practice.q: The **modern Olympic Games** began in —
practice.solution: **1896, Athens** — revived by Pierre de Coubertin; the IOC (1894) is headquartered at **Lausanne**.

practice.q: The Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Communius' adds which idea?
practice.solution: **Communius = 'Together'**, added in 2021 to 'Faster, Higher, Stronger' — the newest static layer of the motto.

practice.q: The first **Winter Olympics** were held at —
practice.solution: **Chamonix, 1924** — the Winter Games run in a separate four-year cycle from the Summer Games.

practice.q: India first participated in the Olympics in —
practice.solution: **1900 Paris** — Norman Pritchard won two athletics silvers; hockey's gold run began only in 1928.

practice.q: How many **Olympic hockey golds** has India won?
practice.solution: **Eight golds** — from Amsterdam 1928 to Moscow 1980, the longest run in Olympic hockey.

practice.q:
Arrange India's sporting firsts chronologically:
1. First Olympic hockey gold 2. First individual Olympic gold 3. First Cricket World Cup win
practice.solution: Hockey gold **1928** → Cricket World Cup **1983** → individual gold (Bindra) **2008**.

practice.q: The **Indian Premier League (IPL)** began in —
practice.solution: The BCCI launched the T20 IPL in **2008** — annual since then.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The first Cricket World Cup was played in 1975.
2. India won the ODI World Cup in 1983 and 2011.
3. The Santosh Trophy is a tennis event.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — the **Santosh Trophy is football** (inter-state championship).

practice.q: **Khelo India Games** were launched in —
practice.solution: **Khelo India (2018)** — annual school and university games to build a sporting pipeline.

practice.q: The **African Union** joined the G20 as a permanent member at the —
practice.solution: At the **New Delhi G20 (2023)** the AU became the second regional bloc (after the EU) with permanent membership.

practice.q: **QUAD** consists of —
practice.solution: The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue groups **India, the USA, Japan and Australia** — revived in 2017, leaders'-level since 2021.

practice.q: **BRICS expansion**, adding members such as Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE, took effect in —
practice.solution: The bloc expanded from January **2024**; South Africa had joined the original BRIC in 2010, and India-Pakistan entered the SCO in 2017 — don't mix the years.

practice.q: The headquarters of **SAARC** is at —
practice.solution: **Kathmandu** hosts SAARC (founded 1985, first summit at Dhaka); BIMSTEC sits at **Dhaka** — don't swap them.

practice.q: **BIMSTEC** groups how many member states?
practice.solution: **Seven** Bay of Bengal littorals — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand; HQ at **Dhaka**.

practice.q: The **ASEAN** secretariat is located at —
practice.solution: ASEAN (Bangkok Declaration, **1967**) works from **Jakarta**; India is a dialogue partner, not a member.

practice.q: Match: 1. SCO 2. SAARC 3. BIMSTEC — with (i) Kathmandu (ii) Beijing (iii) Dhaka:
practice.solution: SCO → **Beijing**; SAARC → **Kathmandu**; BIMSTEC → **Dhaka** — the three HQs exams swap most often.

practice.q: India is **not** a member of —
practice.solution: **APEC** is the classic trap — India is outside it, though it belongs to BRICS, SCO and BIMSTEC.

practice.q: Regarding **ASEAN**, India is —
options: A sectoral dialogue partner, not a member
practice.solution: India partners ASEAN at summit level but is **not** one of its Southeast Asian members — a fixed distinction in every grouping question.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Commonwealth has 56 member states.
2. India is a member of both SAARC and BIMSTEC.
3. India is a member of the G7.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — the **G7 excludes India** (US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada).

practice.q: The **Shanghai Cooperation Organisation** was founded in —
practice.solution: The SCO took its present form in **2001** from the earlier Shanghai Five; India and Pakistan joined as full members in 2017.

practice.q: The **first BRICS summit** was held in —
practice.solution: The acronym ('BRIC') was coined in 2001, but the **first summit came in 2009 at Yekaterinburg**; South Africa joined in 2010.

practice.q:
Arrange by founding year (earliest first):
1. ASEAN 2. SAARC 3. G20
practice.solution: ASEAN **1967** → SAARC **1985** → G20 **1999** (leaders' summits from 2008).

practice.q: The **United Nations** currently has —
practice.solution: **193 members** since South Sudan joined in 2011; 51 states founded the UN in 1945.

practice.q: How many times has India been elected a **non-permanent member** of the UNSC?
practice.solution: **Eight terms** — most recently 2021-22; India campaigns for a permanent seat in the reformed Council.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the UN:
1. It was founded in 1945 with 51 members.
2. The ICJ is its principal judicial organ, seated at The Hague.
3. The UNSC's five permanent members are elected every two years.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong — the **P-5 are permanent** (with veto); only the ten non-permanent seats face election, for two-year terms.

practice.q: **National Youth Day** (12 January) marks the birth anniversary of —
practice.solution: **Swami Vivekananda**, born 12 January 1863 — the day anchors the National Youth Festival.

practice.q: **National Unity Day** (31 October) commemorates —
practice.solution: The **Iron Man's** birth anniversary (31 October 1875) — Rashtriya Ekta Diwas, observed since 2014.

practice.q: **National Education Day** (11 November) honours —
practice.solution: **Maulana Azad**, independent India's first Education Minister, born 11 November 1888 — don't confuse with Teachers' Day (5 September, Radhakrishnan).

practice.q: **National Mathematics Day** (22 December) marks the birth of —
practice.solution: **Ramanujan** (born 22 December 1887); the day has been observed since **2012**, his 125th birth-anniversary year.

practice.q:
Arrange by date within the year:
1. Teachers' Day 2. Children's Day 3. National Sports Day
practice.solution: Sports Day **29 August** → Teachers' Day **5 September** → Children's Day **14 November**.

practice.q: **National Technology Day** (11 May) commemorates —
practice.solution: The **Pokhran-II tests of 11 May 1998**; ISRO-related milestones are marked separately, not on this day.

practice.q: **Constitution Day** (26 November) has been observed since —
practice.solution: The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** and came into force on 26 January 1950; the observance began in **2015** (the 125th birth-anniversary year of Ambedkar).

practice.q: **Navy Day** (4 December) commemorates —
practice.solution: **Operation Trident** — the 1971 missile attack on Karachi harbour; the other operations belong to different services and years.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. National Science Day marks the Raman effect (1928).
2. Army Day is observed on 15 January.
3. Hindi Diwas marks the adoption of Hindi as official language in 1949.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are settled: 28 February (Raman 1928), 15 January (Cariappa 1949), 14 September (1949 resolution).

practice.q: The **International Day of Yoga** (21 June) was first observed in —
practice.solution: The UN declared it in **December 2014** on India's proposal; the first global Yoga Day fell on **21 June 2015**.

practice.q: **World Environment Day** (5 June) traces its origin to —
practice.solution: The UN Conference on the Human Environment at **Stockholm (1972)** both created UNEP and gave the day its start; Rio (1992) came later.

practice.q: **Human Rights Day** (10 December) marks the adoption of —
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
practice.solution: The **UDHR, adopted 10 December 1948** — the UN Charter (1945) and Geneva Conventions are separate instruments.

practice.q: **Indian Air Force Day** is observed on —
practice.solution: **8 October** — the IAF was raised in 1932; 16 December marks Vijay Diwas (1971 victory).

practice.q: Match the service day: 1. Army 2. Air Force 3. Navy — with (i) 8 October (ii) 4 December (iii) 15 January:
practice.solution: Army **15 January** → Air Force **8 October** → Navy **4 December** — chronology makes the trio easy to hold.

practice.q: **Army Day** (15 January) recalls —
options: The raising of the Indian Army
K.M. Cariappa becoming the first Indian Commander-in-Chief
practice.solution: On **15 January 1949** **K.M. Cariappa** took over as the first Indian Commander-in-Chief of the Army.

practice.q: The **Human Development Index (HDI)** is released in the —
practice.solution: The **UNDP's Human Development Report** carries the HDI — health, education and income combined; the WDR belongs to the World Bank and the WEO to the IMF.

practice.q: The **Global Innovation Index** is published by —
practice.solution: **WIPO**, the World Intellectual Property Organization at Geneva, publishes the GII.

practice.q: The **World Happiness Report** is published by —
practice.solution: The **UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network** issues the report each March — not the WHO or the World Bank.

practice.q: Match: 1. HDI 2. World Economic Outlook 3. Global Innovation Index — with (i) IMF (ii) UNDP (iii) WIPO:
practice.solution: HDI → **UNDP**; WEO → **IMF**; GII → **WIPO** — the standard UN-family triple.

practice.q: The **Corruption Perceptions Index** is released by —
practice.solution: **Transparency International (Berlin)** publishes the CPI — higher score means a cleaner public sector.

practice.q: The **Global Peace Index** is released by —
practice.solution: The Sydney-based **IEP**, a think tank — not a UN body; it also issues the Positive Peace report.

practice.q: The **World Press Freedom Index** is compiled by —
practice.solution: **RSF** publishes the annual index each **3 May** — World Press Freedom Day — while UNESCO runs the related prize and day.

practice.q: Which pairing is **wrong**?
options: Environmental Performance Index — Yale and Columbia
practice.solution: The **Global Hunger Index belongs to Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe**, not UNDP — all other pairs are correct.

practice.q: The **SDG India Index** is released by —
practice.solution: **NITI Aayog** tracks states and UTs on the SDGs; MoSPI handles official statistical series instead.

practice.q: The **Annual Status of Education Report (ASER)** is published by —
practice.solution: **Pratham**, an NGO, surveys rural children's reading and arithmetic each year — an outside-the-government report exams quote often.

practice.q: The **Financial Inclusion Index (FI-Index)** is released by —
practice.solution: The **RBI's** FI-Index tracks banking, credit and insurance penetration in one number.

practice.q: The World Bank's **Ease of Doing Business** rankings were discontinued in —
practice.solution: Discontinued in **2021** after a data review; the successor series **Business Ready (B-READY)** began in 2024.

practice.q: The successor to the discontinued **Doing Business** rankings is —
practice.solution: **Business Ready (B-READY)**, first released in **2024** by the World Bank, replaced Doing Business.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The WEF publishes the Global Gender Gap Report.
2. The HDI is published by the World Bank.
3. The India Innovation Index is a NITI Aayog product.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong — the **HDI belongs to the UNDP**, not the World Bank.
practice.shortcut: WEF gender gap; UNDP HDI; NITI innovation.
